chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Fadala ibn Ayyub, from al-Husayn ibn 'Uthman, from Sama'a ibn Mihran, from Abu Basir:

He said: I said to Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him): We travel, and we may encounter a rain puddle near a village in which there is human excrement; a child urinates in it, and a riding animal urinates and defecates in it.

He said: If something stirs in your heart about it, then do this — meaning: part the water with your hand, then perform wudu — for religion is not restrictive; indeed Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says:
«He has not placed upon you in the religion any hardship.» (al-Hajj 22:78)

The correct interpretation of all these narrations is to understand them as referring to water exceeding one kurr; for in that case it does not become impure by what falls into it, unless one of its properties changes, as we have previously established. As for what these narrations contain regarding the command to perform wudu from the side where there is no carcass, or to part the water, this is to be understood as recommended (mustahab) and as a precautionary measure — for the soul finds repulsive touching water adjacent to a carcass, even though its ruling is the ruling of pure water. What indicates this is what we previously cited from the narrations: the threshold of water that is not made impure by anything is water whose volume reaches one kurr; when it falls below that, it becomes impure by what is in it. And what further clarifies this is...

key_terms.التَّنَزُّهِ: precautionary avoidance; refraining from something repugnant even when not legally prohibited
key_terms.الِاسْتِحْبَابِ: mustahab; a recommended but non-obligatory act in Islamic jurisprudence
key_terms.الْغَدِيرِ: rain puddle/pool; a small body of stagnant rainwater near a settlement
key_terms.كُرٍّ: kurr; a unit of water volume (~376 liters) above which still water is not made ritually impure by additions

ai.seo_question: Is rainwater collected in a puddle near a village, contaminated with human and animal waste, considered pure for wudu in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Abu Basir asks Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq (AS) whether travelers may use rain puddles near villages containing human excrement and animal waste for wudu; the Imam permits it, recommending only that one push the water aside with the hand if the heart is troubled, invoking the Quranic principle that religion imposes no hardship. Sheikh al-Tusi appends a legal commentary explaining that all such narrations must be understood as applying to water exceeding one kurr in volume — which does not become ritually impure unless a physical property changes — and that the instruction to part the water is mustahab (recommended), not obligatory.
